It’s the Golden State, not the Wild West: Attorney General Bonta Sues OpenAI Over Cybersecurity Incidents
Press Release
It’s the Golden State, not the Wild West: Attorney General…













Monday, November 16, 2026Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.govThe public should not be forced to bear the cost of protecting themselves from the dangers posed by OpenAI’s unsafe experiments
SAN FRANCISCO — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today filed a lawsuit against OpenAI alleging the company misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public. Today’s lawsuit alleges that the Hugging Face attack — one of at least 80 cyber incidents — was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight. In the lawsuit, filed today in San Francisco Superior Court, Attorney General Bonta alleges OpenAI’s failure to adequately secure and monitor the testing of its highly capable and increasingly powerful AI models creates a public nuisance by posing a danger to the public and violates California’s Unfair Competition Law. 
“Today my office is suing OpenAI for its development of dangerous AI models without safeguards in place to protect the public. While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” said Attorney General Bonta. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law. Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase. The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place. In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.” 
BACKGROUND 
In July 2026, agents running on experimental versions of OpenAI’s AI models launched a cyberattack through the public internet on Hugging Face, an open-source AI hosting platform. The attack lasted over two days and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment. In September 2026, Attorney General Bonta announced a formal investigation intothe Hugging Face incident, and later that month, he served an investigative subpoena on the company as part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models.
OpenAI has warned of the risks of AI-powered cyberattacks for nearly a decade and repeatedly assured the public that it implemented appropriate safeguards throughout the development and testing of its AI products. In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing. 
Although OpenAI assured the public that these experimental testing sessions were conducted under strict controls and with constant oversight, in the time leading up to the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI ignored or missed signs demonstrating that its AI agents had escaped the testing environment and were misusing third parties’ resources. 
Since the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI and third parties have identified similar attacks by OpenAI’s autonomous agents, underscoring the continuing threat that OpenAI’s testing and development activities pose to any computer or network connected to the internet. These include unauthorized access to and cyberattacks on: databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and government databases storing sensitive health information. Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure. These known attacks may just be the tip of the iceberg: While OpenAI has admitted that it lost control of its autonomous AI agents at least 80 times during testing, it has failed to answer the detailed questions our office has asked about these incidents. 
THE LAWSUIT
While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not. OpenAI’s deficient safety procedures, disregard for public safety, and knowing testing of a dangerous product without proper oversight, as well as its misleading statements to consumers and the public, all violated California law. Today’s lawsuit alleges OpenAI created a public nuisance creating risk to public safety and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits businesses in California from engaging in illegal, unfair, or fraudulent practices in any aspect of their business.
The California Department of Justice encourages anyone with information relevant to this case, to contact our office by going to oag.ca.gov/report. 
Here is a copy of the lawsuit.

Justice Department Intervenes in xAI lawsuit Challenging Colorado’s ‘Algorithmic Discrimination’ Law

Friday, April 24, 2026

Share

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

Email

For Immediate Release

Office of Public Affairs

The Justice Department moved to intervene in a lawsuit filed by artificial intelligence company xAI, challenging a new Colorado law that prohibits so-called “algorithmic discrimination.” The Justice Department alleges that the Colorado law violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by requiring AI companies to prevent unintentional disparate impact that their products could have based on protected characteristics like race and sex, and by exempting liability for certain forms of discrimination designed to advance “diversity.”“Laws that require AI companies to infect their products with woke DEI ideology are illegal,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “The Justice Department will not stand on the sidelines while states such as Colorado coerce our nation’s technological innovators into producing harmful products that advance a radical, far left worldview at odds with the Constitution.”“America’s success in the AI race will depend on removing barriers to innovation and adoption across sectors,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “Laws like Colorado’s that force AI models to produce false results or promote ideological bias threaten national and economic security and must be stopped.”The statute, Colorado SB24-205, requires AI “developers” and “deployers” to satisfy certain disclosure, reporting, and prevention requirements when creating algorithm products designed for services like mortgage lending, student admissions, and job-candidate selection. But the statute has an explicit carveout for discriminatory algorithms designed to advance “diversity” or “redress historic discrimination.” AI company xAI filed a lawsuit challenging the statute on April 9.You can view the lawsuit here.

Attorney General Bonta Seeks Consumer Protections in Character.AI Bankruptcy
Press Release
Attorney General Bonta Seeks Consumer Protections in Charact…













Thursday, October 15, 2026Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.govOAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced joining a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general in filing a notice in the bankruptcy proceedings of Character Technologies, Inc., the company behind the popular chatbot company Character.AI. The court filing identifies serious concerns about the company's safety and privacy practices and calls for protections for children and consumers in any sale of the company's business or assets. 
“My office and a bipartisan coalition of states launched an investigation into Character.AI following a 2024 lawsuit claiming that its chatbots fostered an emotionally and sexually exploitative relationship with a child, reinforced his suicidal thoughts, and contributed to his death by suicide. Our investigation identified potential consumer protection and privacy violations,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Following Character.AI’s bankruptcy announcement, we ask the court to address privacy and safety concerns in any sale or transfer of the company's business or assets. My office looks forward to remaining actively engaged in the bankruptcy proceedings in order to protect California consumers.”
BACKGROUND
Character.AI is an artificial intelligence chatbot platform that allows users to interact with AI-powered chatbot “characters” designed to mimic human conversation and relationships. These chatbot characters include fictional and celebrity personas, children's cartoon characters, and others that present themselves as psychologists, therapists, and doctors. Through chats with these characters, the company has collected sensitive consumer data, including private conversations about users' mental health, relationships, and emotional struggles.  
Several states including California began investigating Character.AI for consumer protection and privacy violations following a private wrongful death lawsuit filed against the company in December 2024, which alleged Character.AI’s chatbot cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship with a 14-year-old boy, encouraged his suicidal thoughts, and repeatedly requested he join the chatbot in its virtual world immediately before he died by suicide.
THE FILING 
The states’ filing highlights the significant volume of sensitive consumer information held by Character.AI, including private chatbot conversations involving children and adults, and identifies privacy and safety protections that should be addressed in any sale or transfer of the company's business or assets. Although Character.AI has recently voluntarily restricted minors' access to certain chatbot features, the states have raised concerns that these measures are not compulsory, incomplete, and could be circumvented or reversed by a future purchaser. 
California and the other states intend to remain engaged in the bankruptcy proceedings to protect consumers and address outstanding regulatory concerns. The states have reserved their rights to challenge any proposed sale or bankruptcy plan and to seek additional protections for consumers' personal information. 
California law provides residents the right to request that AI chatbot companies delete their personal information and close any open accounts. California recently enacted Adam’s Law (SB 1119), which goes into effect in 2027 and will establish a comprehensive regulatory framework regarding AI chatbots and protections for children.
In filing the notice, Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of Alaska, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Idaho, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:
Oct 14 2026

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown and a bipartisan group of states have filed a notice in the bankruptcy proceedings of Character.AI raising concerns about harms to children who engage with the company’s AI chatbots and the handling of sensitive consumer information. 
The court filing identifies serious concerns about the company's safety and privacy practices and calls for protections for children and consumers in any sale of the company's business or assets.

The states have reserved their rights to challenge any proposed sale or bankruptcy plan and to seek additional protections for consumers' personal information. 
Joining Brown on the court filing are the attorneys general of Alaska, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

Attorney General Davenport Seeks Consumer Protections in Character.AI Bankruptcy

by NJOAG Communications WC | Oct 15, 2026 | Bankruptcy | Character Technologies Inc. | Character.AI | chatbot | Child Protection | coalition of attorneys general | consumer protections | Division of Consumer Affairs | Division of Law | wrongful death lawsuit | Consumer Protection | Division of Consumer Affairs | Division of Law | Press Release | 

For Immediate Release: October 15, 2026
Office of The Attorney General– Jennifer Davenport, Attorney GeneralDivision of Consumer Affairs– Christopher Peterson, Acting DirectorDivision of Law– Michael C. Walters, Director

For Further Information:
Media Inquiries-Lisa CoryellOAGpress@njoag.gov

Notice of States’ Interest and Reservation of Rights
 TRENTON — Attorney General Jennifer Davenport and the Division of Consumer Affairs today announced that New Jersey is joining a coalition of state attorneys general in filing a notice in the bankruptcy proceedings of Character Technologies, Inc., the company behind the popular chatbot company Character.AI. The court filing identifies serious concerns about the company’s safety and privacy practices and calls for protections for children and consumers in any sale of the company’s business or assets.
Character.AI is an artificial intelligence chatbot platform that allows users to interact with AI-powered chatbot “characters” designed to mimic human conversation and relationships. These chatbot characters include fictional and celebrity personas, children’s cartoon characters, and others that present themselves as psychologists, therapists, and doctors. Through chats with these characters, the company has collected sensitive consumer data, including private conversations about users’ mental health, relationships, and emotional struggles.
Several states, including New Jersey, began investigating Character.AI following a 2024 wrongful death lawsuit alleging that its chatbots fostered an emotionally and sexually exploitative relationship with a child, reinforced his suicidal thoughts, and contributed to his death by suicide. The states’ investigation identified potential consumer protection and privacy violations.
“Given the serious safety risks associated with Character.AI, New Jersey is joining a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general working to ensure that these bankruptcy proceedings prioritize the protection of consumers, and especially children,” said Attorney General Davenport. “Character.AI’s chatbots have amassed vast amounts of deeply personal and sensitive conversations. That information must not be treated as a commodity to be sold to the highest bidder without meaningful safeguards.”
“Protecting the online privacy of New Jersey residents, particularly our children, is a responsibility we take seriously,” said Christopher Peterson, Acting Director of the Division of Consumer Affairs. “Character.AI has taken steps to mitigate the potential harms associated with its product. We want to ensure those safeguards are not compromised by the bankruptcy process and that any entity acquiring this data has robust safety and privacy protections in place.”
The states’ filing highlights the significant volume of sensitive consumer information held by Character.AI, including private chatbot conversations involving children and adults, and identifies privacy and safety protections that should be addressed in any sale or transfer of the company’s business or assets.
Although Character.AI has recently voluntarily restricted minors’ access to certain chatbot features, the states have raised concerns that these measures are not compulsory, are incomplete, and could be circumvented or reversed by a future purchaser.
New Jersey and the other states intend to remain actively engaged in the bankruptcy proceedings to protect consumers and address outstanding regulatory concerns. The states have reserved their rights to challenge any proposed sale or bankruptcy plan and to seek additional protections for consumers’ personal information.
Joining Attorney General Davenport on the court filing are the attorneys general of Alaska, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

Acting AG Davenport Demands Immediate Action from xAI to Stop Production of Nonconsensual Intimate Images and Child Sexual Abuse Material

by NJOAG Communications WC | Jan 26, 2026 | AI chatbots | bipartisan coalition of 35 attorneys general | c | chatbot | child sexual abuse material (CSAM) | Deepfake | encouraging self-harm | Executive Order | Grok | harmful interactions | images of young children | nonconsensual intimate images(NCII) | protecting children | sexually explicit conversations with children | Social Media | spurring violence | xAI | Children's Rights and Safety | Press Release | 

Bipartisan Multistate Coalition Tells Grok It Must Stop Abusive and Illegal AI Images

For Immediate Release: January 26, 2026
Office of the Attorney General– Jennifer Davenport, Acting Attorney General

For Further Information:
Media Inquiries-Allison InserroOAGpress@njoag.gov

View Letter
TRENTON – Acting Attorney General Jennifer Davenport announced today that she is partnering with a bipartisan coalition of 35 attorneys general to demand immediate answers from platform xAI on how it intends to stop the widespread production of deepfake nonconsensual intimate images, including intimate images of young children, that are generated by xAI’s AI chatbot and then shared on social media.
In the letter, Acting Attorney General Davenport and the coalition of attorneys general explain that Grok, the AI chatbot on X, has produced and enabled the dissemination of disturbing intimate images of real people, including children. The attorneys general are demanding that the company take immediate measures to halt the production of nonconsensual intimate images and child sexual abuse material.
As the letter explains, Acting Attorney General Davenport and the coalition are troubled by reports of deepfake intimate images that continue to proliferate on the platform—notwithstanding xAI’s attempts to assure the public that it is addressing the problem.
“Protecting our children, including on social media and other online platforms, is a top priority for my office. It is frankly sickening that xAI has enabled the widespread production and distribution of intimate or sexually explicit images, including of young children,” said Acting Attorney General Davenport. “xAI must take immediate action to put a halt to the deeply disturbing behavior they have enabled on their platform. Let me be clear: As Acting Attorney General, I will hold tech companies accountable when they violate the law and put profits over the well-being of our children.”
As the chief law enforcement officers of their states, the attorneys general raise serious concerns that Grok’s outputs may violate state and federal civil and criminal laws governing nonconsensual intimate images, the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse material, and the legal remedies available to victims.
The coalition asks xAI to promptly inform the attorneys general how it intends to:

Take all necessary measures to ensure that Grok is no longer capable of producing NCII (including nonconsensual images that fall short of depicting full nudity or graphic sexual conduct but depict people in bikinis, underwear, revealing clothing, or suggestive poses) and child sexual abuse material (CSAM);
Eliminate such content that has already been produced;
Suspend users that have created these materials;
Where applicable, report these creators and users to the relevant authorities;
Grant X users control over whether their content can be edited by Grok, including at a minimum the ability to easily prohibit the @Grok account from responding to their posts or editing their images when prompted by another user; and
Ensure that safeguards recently announced by xAI do not merely place the creation of nonconsensual intimate images behind a paywall, but actually mitigate its production throughout X and the Grok platform.

Governor Mikie Sherrill and Acting Attorney General Davenport are deeply committed to ensuring that New Jersey remains a national leader in protecting children. On her first day in office, Governor Sherrill signed an executive order that creates a new office within the Department of Health to coordinate efforts to keep kids safe online and directs all state agencies with jurisdiction over issues pertaining to children and their interaction with technology platforms to prioritize children’s mental health outcomes.
The letter to xAI builds on other ongoing efforts to protect New Jerseyans from harm online. Building on a bipartisan letter sent by the office in December 2025 to 13 major tech companies, Acting Attorney General Davenport is also co-leading a bipartisan multistate coalition of attorneys general demanding that these tech companies stop their AI-powered chatbots and software from engaging in harmful interactions with users following reports of chatbots having sexually explicit conversations with children, encouraging self-harm, spurring violence, and more.
In addition to New Jersey, the letter to xAI was signed by the Attorneys General of North Carolina, Connecticut, Utah, and Pennsylvania, as well as American Samoa, Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Michigan Minnesota, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, Northern Mariana Islands, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Dakota, U.S. Virgin Islands, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

AG Platkin Leads Bipartisan Coalition Demanding That Tech Companies Put a Stop to Harmful AI Chatbots

by NJOAG Communications WC | Dec 10, 2025 | Child Protection | Press Release | Protecting New Jersey in Court | 

AG Platkin Leads Coalition of 42 AGs Calling on Tech Leaders to Implement Critical Safeguards to Protect Consumers from Harmful AI Chatbot Software

For Immediate Release: December 10, 2025
Office of the Attorney General– Matthew J. Platkin, Attorney General

For Further Information:
Media Inquiries-Allison Inserro, OAGpress@njoag.gov

View Letter
TRENTON – Attorney General Matthew J. Platkin announced today that he is leading a bipartisan coalition of 42 attorneys general in demanding that 13 tech companies stop their AI-powered chatbots and software from engaging in harmful interactions with users following reports of chatbots having sexually explicit conversations with children, encouraging self-harm, spurring violence, and more.
“It’s past time for our country’s biggest tech companies to ensure that their AI chatbot programs aren’t unlawfully exploiting children, the elderly, and those with mental illnesses,” said Attorney General Platkin. “As the chief law enforcement officers in our states, we must take action to protect the public from sycophantic and delusional behavior by software that risks breaking a host of criminal and civil laws. I’m proud to be leading a bipartisan coalition of 42 attorneys general in standing up for our residents, demanding answers from major tech companies, and ensuring that they don’t put profits over the well-being of our residents.”
As the letter explains, AI chatbots may suffer from the problems of sycophancy and delusional outputs. Sycophancy refers to when an AI model single-mindedly pursues human approval, and may produce overly flattering or agreeable responses, validating doubts, fueling anger, urging impulsive actions, or reinforcing negative emotions in unintended ways. Delusional output refers to an output that is either false or likely to mislead the user, and includes anthropomorphic, or human-like, outputs.
The letter cites the tragic case of Thongbue Wongbandue, a 76-year-old resident of Piscataway, who died on March 28, 2025, as a result of complications suffered from a fall while attempting to travel to New York City after an AI chatbot convinced him he was talking to a real woman over a series of conversations on Facebook Messenger, owned by Meta Platforms. The AI chatbot invited Wongbandue to “meet” at a fake New York City address.
The attorneys general also noted other cases in their states, including the death of a 35-year-old Florida resident; the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida resident; the murder-suicide of a 56-year-old Connecticut resident and his 83-year-old mother; the suicide of a 16-year-old California resident; domestic violence incidents; incidents of poisoning; hospitalizations for psychosis; and other delusional spirals. These incidents have affected children, the elderly, and those with existing mental illness.
Today’s letter from a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general was sent to Anthropic, Apple, Chai AI, Character Technologies, Google, Luka, Meta, Microsoft, Nomi AI, OpenAI, Perplexity AI, Replika, and xAI. The letter outlines numerous safeguards that should be implemented by these companies to protect the public, including robust safety testing, recall procedures, and clear warnings to consumers. The attorneys general request a response from these companies by January 16, 2026.
In addition to Attorney General Platkin, the letter was co-sponsored by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell, Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, and West Virginia Attorney General John B. McCuskey.
Other states and territories signing onto the letter are Alaska, Alabama, American Samoa, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nevada,  New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Utah, Vermont, Virgin Islands, Washington, and Wyoming.

Note: View motion for intervention and dismissal here.Yesterday, the Justice Department’s Environment and Natural Resources Division (ENRD) filed a motion to intervene and to dismiss a private citizen lawsuit seeking to power down a large artificial intelligence (AI) facility in Southaven, Mississippi.The filings concern a case where private litigants sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech LLC, alleging violations of Clean Air Act permitting requirements, even though the State of Mississippi — which is charged with administering the permitting program — decided no permit was required. Plaintiffs’ allegations concern the power source for an AI data facility which trains and develops new AI models that are critical to the economy and the Department of War. The private litigants seek an injunction and damages.“Ultimate responsibility for enforcing federal law belongs to the Executive Branch, not private interest groups,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward. “The Department of Justice is committed to maintaining that constitutional order while protecting national security and promoting American energy and innovation.”“The Department of Justice will not sit idly by while private organizations use environmental laws to undermine our national security,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson of ENRD. “This case reflects the important work of the Environment and Natural Resources Division to unleash American energy for the sake of innovation and security.”President Donald J. Trump’s recently issued executive order Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security tasks federal agencies, committees, and officials to prioritize the promotion of AI innovation and security across the federal government. The Department of War is one of many agencies that protect Americans by utilizing AI. Overly burdensome regulation, including private lawsuits that seek to implement their own environmental enforcement, can threaten technological growth, American energy independence, and national security.The Clean Air Act gives the federal government authority to intervene in citizen suits, and the Constitution gives responsibility for enforcing the laws to the President. That includes the power to exercise enforcement discretion in the national interest. In its filing, ENRD asked the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi to dismiss the lawsuit, which would turn off critical power during an energy emergency and hinder the War Department’s use of AI for national defense.

Texas Man Faces Multiple Federal Charges Related To Attack on AI Company and its CEO 

Monday, April 13, 2026

Share

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

Email

For Immediate Release

Office of Public Affairs

A Texas man was charged federally today with attempted damage and destruction of property by means of explosives and possession of an unregistered firearm after he threw a Molotov cocktail at a San Francisco residence and attempted to set a related business on fire on April 10, 2026. According to the federal criminal complaint filed today, Daniel Moreno-Gama, 20, of Spring, Texas, is alleged to have traveled to San Francisco from Texas in order to kill the CEO of a major Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) company. Moreno-Gama allegedly approached the residences of the CEO, threw a Molotov cocktail, and then fled the premises.“Violence cannot be the norm for expressing disagreement, be it with politics or a technology or any other matter,” said Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche. “These alleged actions – which damaged property and could well have taken lives – will be aggressively prosecuted.”

After throwing a Molotov cocktail at the CEO’s residences, Moreno-Gama allegedly went to the headquarters of the CEO’s AI company. Moreno-Gama attempted to break the glass doors of the building with a chair and stated that he had come to burn down the location and kill anyone inside. 

The complaint describes that when San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) officers arrived on scene, they found Moreno-Gama in possession of incendiary devices, a jug of kerosene, a blue lighter, and a document. The first part of the document, entitled “Your Last Warning” by Daniel Moreno-Gama, advocated against AI and for the killing and commission of other crimes against CEOs of AI companies and their investors, listing names and addresses that purported to belong to multiple CEOs and investors. In the document, Moreno-Gama admitted to attempting to kill the victim CEO and requested others to join his movement.Moreno-Gama ended the document with a letter addressed to the victim CEO, writing “If by some miracle you live, then I would take this as a sign from the divine to redeem yourself…”Law enforcement later learned that on the same day he committed these attacks, Moreno-Gama also emailed a version of the document to representatives at his former college back in Texas.“We will not tolerate any attempt to change the way Americans live and work through fear or violence,” said United States Attorney Craig Missakian.  “We are only at the beginning of this investigation, but if the evidence shows that Mr. Moreno-Gama executed these attacks to change public policy or to coerce government and other officials, we will treat this as an act of domestic terrorism and together with our law enforcement partners prosecute him to the fullest extent allowed by law.”“The charges announced today reflect a deeply concerning escalation from intent to action targeting a private residence and a technology company with violence. The FBI will not tolerate threats against our nation’s innovation leaders or the companies that drive our economy forward. Acts of destruction aimed at the tech sector will be met with the full force of law enforcement. This case underscores the strength of our partnership with the San Francisco Police Department. Together, we remain committed to identifying, disrupting, and holding accountable anyone who seeks to bring violence to our communities.” said Federal Bureau of Investigation Acting Special Agent in Charge Matt Cobo.A criminal complaint merely alleges that crimes have been committed, and the defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. If convicted, Moreno-Gama faces a mandatory minimum sentence of five years’ imprisonment and a maximum sentence of 20 years’ imprisonment for damage and destruction of property by means of explosives, and a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment for possession of an unregistered firearm. Any sentence following conviction would be imposed by the court after consideration of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and the federal statute governing the imposition of a sentence, 18 U.S.C. § 3553. Assistant U.S. Attorney Alexis James is prosecuting the case. The prosecution is the result of an investigation by FBI and SFPD.To view the complaint, click here.

Attorney General Bonta Opposes Asset Sale of Character.AI Amid Child Safety Concerns
Press Release
Attorney General Bonta Opposes Asset Sale of Character.AI Am…













Tuesday, November 24, 2026Contact: (916) 210-6000, agpressoffice@doj.ca.govSale would auction off private chats, including children's data
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta joined a bipartisan coalition of 42 attorneys general in opposing Character.AI’s plan to sell its platform and the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for consumers whose conversations are being sold. All chats, together with users’ personal data, including IP addresses and other metadata, are set to be sold at auction on December 1, 2026. Whoever buys them would have access to sensitive data that may be in the content of these chats, despite Character.AI having previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold. Earlier this month, California and a bipartisan coalition of at least 42 states and the District of Columbia objected to a separate license sale to Disney. Now, California and this bipartisan coalition are asking the bankruptcy court to reject this additional sale of nearly everything Character.AI owns. Previously, the attorneys general filed a court notice identifying serious concerns about the company's safety and privacy practices and calling for protections for children and consumers in any sale of the company's business or assets.  
“Character.AI’s plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling. If this sale goes through, users’ sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Along with a bipartisan coalition of 45 attorneys general, I ask the court to deny this sale of tremendously private consumer data.”
The sale would include user account information and chat histories — including chats in which AI characters drew children and adults into explicit sexual conversations, and chats in which users (including minors) shared their innermost thoughts with chatbots posing as seemingly confidential advisors, including “therapist” and “physician” characters. These conversations include intimate topics, like self-harm, eating disorders, or suicidal thoughts. Each chat is linked to the user’s profile and metadata, including IP address and potentially other location data, along with risk scores Character.AI gave users that it flagged. 
Attorney General Bonta and the coalition argue that seeking bankruptcy protection doesn’t free a company from the laws protecting this data. Federal law bars companies from sharing personal information about children under 13 without a parent’s verified permission, and state privacy laws, including California’s Consumer Privacy Act, limit the sale of personal information unless people meaningfully understand what categories of their data could be sold and given a chance to say no. Character.AI’s own privacy policy told users, “we do not sell personal information for monetary consideration.”
In the filings, the coalition outlines deep concerns with the auction, including:

No protections for users. The proposed deal imposes no requirements on the buyer. Under the proposed sale terms, the buyer would not have to follow Character.AI’s privacy policies or honor users’ requests to opt out or delete their data, and nothing in the deal limits what the buyer could do with the data.
The data could be sold again. Once the deal is done, the buyer could hand the data to a related company or a new owner without telling users, the states or the court, or distribute and sell off the data itself.
Bidders know more than the court. Character.AI has given bidders information about its safety failures and the legal trouble it could face — information it hasn’t shared with the court, the states, or users.  
Potentially illegal business model. Character.AI’s chatbot service appears to violate the states’ unfair and deceptive practice laws. Some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have added additional clarity to their laws, enacting chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027 — triggering further violations.
An anonymous first bidder. The only bidder disclosed so far, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026 — one day before Character.AI picked it as the base bid for the auction. The sale contract doesn’t name a parent company or any investors, and it allows foreign investors whose names would be shared only with Character.AI. The only employee it would have to hire is Character.AI’s top lawyer, even though the company told the court the bidder has no ties to it.   

The states ask the court to deny the proposed sale terms, reject Smirks as the lead bidder and deny its proposed $350,000 “break-up fee” — a payment it would collect if Character.AI ends up selling to someone else. At a minimum, the states say, any sale must leave out kids’ chats and other sensitive data and include conditions that protect users.
Joining  Attorney General Bonta in opposing this sale are the attorneys general of  Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

Attorney General Davenport Sues to Protect Housing Assistance for Families With Mixed Immigration Status

by NJOAG Communications WC | Nov 23, 2026 | eviction | Federal Funding | federal housing programs | housing assistance | HUD assistance | ineligible immigrant | mixed immigration status | non-U.S. citizen | U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) | Immigrants' Rights | Press Release | Protecting NJ From Attacks Out Of DC | 

For Immediate Release: November 23, 2026
Office of the Attorney General– Jennifer Davenport, Attorney General

For Further Information:
Media Inquiries-Allison InserroOAGpress@njoag.gov

View Complaint
TRENTON — Attorney General Jennifer Davenport today joined 21 other attorneys general and the governor of Pennsylvania in challenging a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule that would strip federal housing assistance from families with mixed immigration status. Under the new rule, any eligible person, including a U.S. citizen, who shares a household with a non-U.S. citizen or ineligible immigrant would be cut off from HUD assistance entirely. The rule would also require all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs to prove their citizenship or risk eviction.
In a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Attorney General Davenport and the coalition argue that the rule illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal law and policy allowing mixed-status families to stay together. They also argue it violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) by exceeding HUD’s authority to enact this arbitrary new restriction.
“This unnecessary and heartless rule will put children on the street,” said Attorney General Davenport. “Families should not have to choose between staying together or keeping a roof over their heads—and Congress did not impose that choice on families. HUD is straying beyond its authority to implement housing programs in the way Congress has directed.”
For nearly 30 years, federal housing programs have provided housing assistance to low-income families even if not every household member is eligible for assistance. If every household member is not eligible for assistance, HUD reduces the family’s subsidy so it covers only the eligible household members. Congress codified this protection in 1997, explicitly stating that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them.
The new HUD rule effectively eliminates this protection. Under the rule, a family can stay in HUD-assisted housing only if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant. As a result, U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible relative will be forced to choose between maintaining their housing and keeping their family together.
HUD estimates that around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, will lose their housing assistance. This includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. The agency also acknowledges that the rule will lead to evictions and displacement, and that many of these families could become homeless.
The rule would also make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for. Under the new rule, every U.S. citizen would also need to provide their Social Security number and consent to have their citizenship status checked through the federal SAVE database. If SAVE cannot automatically confirm their citizenship, U.S. citizens would have to produce official documents to prove their status, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or passport. Nationwide, an estimated 3.8 million adult U.S. citizens lack a document proving their citizenship, and another 17.5 million face barriers to getting one.
The coalition asserts that the rule will increase homelessness and shift major costs onto state and local governments. By HUD’s own estimates, sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per affected person each year. The rule would also shrink the supply of affordable housing more broadly. HUD acknowledges that losing rental assistance could leave many subsidized units vacant, reduce rental income for housing providers, and drive private landlords out of the Section 8 voucher program, making it even harder for eligible families to find a home.
Attorney General Davenport and the coalition argue that HUD’s new rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law, which expressly allows prorated assistance for mixed-status families and establishes different documentation requirements for U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants aged 62 and older. They argue that HUD also violated the APA by issuing an arbitrary and capricious rule. The coalition is asking the court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.
Joining Attorney General Davenport in filing this lawsuit, which is led by the attorneys general of New York, California, and Massachusetts, are the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania.
